fact: A process model is a graphical representation of how a business system should operate, illustrating the processes and activities performed and how data move among them

A process model can document the current system, called the AS-IS system, or the new system being developed, called the TO-BE system; modelling as-is helps identify inefficiencies, delays or redundancies so an improved to-be model can enhance performance, reduce cost and increase productivity

A BUSINESS PROCESS is a collection of activities designed to produce a specific output for a particular customer or market; it emphasises HOW the work is done within an organisation, in contrast to a product, which focuses on WHAT

A PROCESS is a set of related activities or tasks performed in sequence to achieve a specific goal or produce a desired output, involving inputs, actions and outputs; it is a specific ordering of work activities across time and place, with a beginning, an end, and clearly defined inputs and outputs, that is a structure for action
A MODEL is a pictorial representation of reality

PROCESS MODELLING is a technique for organising and documenting a system's processes, inputs, outputs and data stores; it is a formal and graphical way of representing how a business operates, and its main tool is the Data Flow Diagram

The importance of process modelling: it lets designers and users focus on the business aspects of systems; it helps developers understand user requirements, design system functionality and ensure the system meets business needs; it is cheap and easy to modify, especially with CASE tools; its non-technical notation is easily understood by business people; DFDs allow isolation of parts of the system at any chosen level of detail; and process models act as formal documentation of how a system or business operates

A Data Flow Diagram shows business processes and the data that flows between them, depicting the flow of data through a system and the work or processing performed by that system; it shows the source of data input, the processes that act on the data, and the data store, without technical details such as programming
DFDs allow the analyst to determine what the organisation does and how the organisation does it

DFDs are purely logical, not physical models; they contain no implementation details; the DFD is drawn first because it lets designers and users concentrate purely on capturing business aspects; and it is not contaminated by distractions of technical details
There are FOUR DFD elements: external agent or entity, data flow, process, and data store

An EXTERNAL ENTITY is a person, organisation or system outside the system boundary that interacts with the system, and is the source and destination of data; it is depicted as a RECTANGLE, named with a descriptive singular NOUN such as Student, Customer, Client or employee, and it does NOT perform processing

DATA FLOWS are directed arrows, also described as pipes, and data flows in packets through them; one flow arrow represents the movement of multiple data items; names should connote the actual information, such as Order Details or Receipt, and are NOUNS

A PROCESS is depicted by a rectangle with round edges and represents an activity or operation that transforms input data into output data; the data flowing out has more value after processing, and a process is always active; examples are Create Student Record, Calculate Purchase Cost and Register Client
A process name must contain VERBS and must NOT be procedural; the manual's own example contrasts 'Add 1 to the counter', which is procedural, with 'Increment counter', which is a process

Hints to identify a logical process: it performs computations; it makes decisions; it sorts, filters or otherwise summarises data; it organises data into useful information; it triggers other processes; and it uses stored data, that is creates, reads, updates or deletes a record

A DATA STORE is a place where data is stored for later use; the data never changes in the store except that it is used as input to a process and the updated data is returned; naming avoids verbs and physical descriptions of how the data is stored, for example Student Master or Client List; it is frequently implemented as a file or database
A data store is DATA AT REST compared with a data flow, which is DATA IN MOTION; a data store is represented as an open-ended rectangle, that is two parallel lines
The notation described is the GANE-SARSON notation; another popular notation is the DeMarco and Yourdon symbol set

DECOMPOSITION is the iterative act of going from one single system to many component processes, breaking a complex system into smaller, more detailed sub-processes, so the analyst moves from a high-level overview to a detailed understanding; each level of abstraction reveals more or fewer details

The CONTEXT DIAGRAM represents the entire system as one single process and shows the data flows to and from external entities; data stores are usually NOT included unless they are owned by systems or processes other than the one being documented; it shows only external entities and the data flows in and out of the system

The LEVEL 0 DFD breaks the main system into major sub-processes, representing the system's major processes, data flows and data stores at a higher level; it shows all the processes that comprise the overall system and adds data stores; ALL PROCESS MODELS HAVE EXACTLY ONE LEVEL 0 DFD

LEVEL 1 and lower levels further break down each process into more detailed sub-processes, continuing until the process is simple enough to understand; for example Withdraw Money breaks into Validate PIN, Check Balance and Dispense Cash
When decomposing a DFD you must CONSERVE inputs and outputs from processes at the higher level of decomposition; this is called BALANCING, and it ensures consistency across all levels

The manual's worked ATM example builds a Process 0 context diagram with the Customer as the only entity, then a Level 0 showing major processes such as Authenticate User, Withdraw Money, Deposit Money and Check Balance with their data stores and flows, then a Level 1 decomposing Withdraw Money
